title: Atomic commits: one commit, one change
objective: By the end of this lesson you can build a history where each commit does exactly one thing, and you can use that history to find a bug automatically instead of by guesswork.

blocks.text: An atomic commit contains one complete change and nothing else. Not one file — one change, which may touch several files. The test is simple: could this commit be reverted on its own without breaking something unrelated, and does its message describe a single thing?

rows: Add upload limit, fix typo, reformat file, bump version
Fix timezone shift on the report export
Half a feature that does not run
A working slice, even if small
A rename mixed into a behaviour change
The rename alone, then the behaviour change

blocks.title: Why the mixed commit hurts later
blocks.text: When the upload limit turns out to be wrong, you want to revert it. If the same commit also reformatted a file and bumped a version, reverting takes those with it — so you end up doing surgery on a commit instead of reverting it. Atomic commits are what make revert a real option rather than a theoretical one.
Separating a rename from a behaviour change

This is the highest-value habit in the whole lesson. A commit that renames a function across forty files produces an enormous diff that a reviewer cannot read. The same commit with two changed lines of logic buried inside it hides the only part that matters.

blocks.caption: Two commits, both readable
lines: git commit -m "Rename calculateTotal to calculateOrderTotal"   # 40 files, zero behaviour change
git commit -m "Include tax in the order total"                  # 2 lines, all the meaning
# The reviewer skims the first and reads the second carefully.
# One commit containing both gets a shallow review of everything.

blocks.text: Building atomic commits from messy work
You do not have to work in a tidy order. Work however you think, then shape the commits afterwards — which is exactly what the staging area and interactive rebase are for.

blocks.caption: Splitting what you already did
lines: git add -p             # stage change by change: y, n, s to split a hunk further
git commit -m "Reject uploads over 10MB"
git add -p             # now stage the next distinct change
git commit -m "Log rejected uploads with their size"
git rebase -i HEAD~5   # or reshape commits you already made

blocks.title: Every commit should leave the project working
blocks.text: If a commit leaves tests failing, later tools cannot use your history: a bisect will land on it and report a false result, and a revert will produce a broken state. 'Working' can mean small — a slice with its test — but it should not mean 'half a rename'.
The payoff: finding a bug automatically

git bisect performs a binary search through your history. You tell it a commit where the bug exists and one where it does not; it checks out the middle commit, you say whether the bug is present, and it halves the range each time. Twenty commits take five checks. A thousand take ten.

blocks.caption: A manual bisect
lines: git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # the current commit has the bug
git bisect good v2.3.0         # this released version did not
# Git checks out a commit in the middle. Test it, then:
git bisect bad     # or: git bisect good
# repeat until Git names the first bad commit
git bisect reset               # return to where you started

blocks.caption: An automatic bisect
lines: git bisect start HEAD v2.3.0
git bisect run npm test -- upload.test.js
# Git runs the command at each step and reads the exit code:
# 0 = good, non-zero = bad. It reports the first bad commit unattended.

blocks.title: Bisect is only as good as the history
blocks.text: It assumes each commit builds and runs. A history full of half-finished commits produces a bisect that stops on one of them and blames it — you have found where the tree was broken, not where the bug was introduced. This is the concrete reason atomic commits are worth the discipline.

blocks.title: Split a messy change, then bisect for a bug
steps: In ~/git-lab: make two unrelated edits to one file — one you would call a fix, one you would call a rename
Run: git add -p        (stage only the fix; answer n to the other hunk)
Run: git commit -m "Fix the limit check"
Run: git add -p && git commit -m "Rename the helper"
Run: git log --oneline -3   (two commits, each doing one thing)
Now create a bug to find: make five commits, one of which writes a wrong value into a file
Run: git bisect start HEAD HEAD~5
At each step check the file and answer git bisect good or git bisect bad
blocks.expected: One messy working state turned into two commits that each say one thing, then a deliberately planted bug located by binary search in about three checks instead of five manual inspections.

cheatsheet: Atomic = one complete change, possibly across several files
Test: could this be reverted alone, and does one sentence describe it?
Separate a rename from a behaviour change — always
Every commit should leave the project in a working state
git add -p stages change by change (y / n / s to split further)
git rebase -i reshapes commits you already made
git bisect start / bad / good — binary search for the commit that introduced a bug
git bisect run <command> — fully automatic, using the exit code
git bisect reset returns you to where you started
Bisect only works on a history where each commit runs

choices.B: It contains one complete change — possibly across several files — that could be reverted on its own

checkpoint.explanation: The unit is the change, not the file. A single coherent change often touches a handful of files together.

checkpoint.prompt: Why separate a large rename from a small behaviour change?

choices.A: Git handles renames faster in isolation
choices.B: Mixed together, the two lines that matter are invisible inside a forty-file diff, so the review is shallow
choices.D: It is required by most platforms

checkpoint.explanation: Reviewers skim mechanical changes and read logic changes. Combining them means the logic gets skimmed too.

choices.B: Performs a binary search through history to find the commit that introduced a bug
choices.C: Divides a branch into two branches

checkpoint.explanation: You mark a good and a bad commit; it halves the range at each step. A thousand commits take about ten checks.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does bisect fail on a history of half-finished commits?

choices.A: It refuses to run on branches
choices.B: It assumes every commit builds and runs; if one does not, bisect stops there and blames a commit that was merely broken, not the one that introduced the bug
choices.C: It only works on the main branch

checkpoint.explanation: This is the practical payoff of the discipline: a history where each commit works is a history you can search automatically.
